item.title: [Itrfoundation] Listening, Learning, and Bringing the Taxpayer’s Voice to Local Government
item.description:
ITR Foundation's second annual Local Government Symposium brought together local officials, policy experts, retired public servants, and taxpayers for thoughtful discussions on the challenges facing Iowa's cities, counties, and schools. Rather than offering one-size-fits-all solutions for Iowa’s unique communities, the symposium encouraged local leaders to question assumptions, explore new ideas, and consider practical approaches to budgeting, governance, communication, and public policy. Throughout each discussion, the taxpayer's perspective was emphasized: local government budgets should not grow faster than taxpayers' ability to pay, and lasting fiscal health requires balancing the needs of government with the financial realities facing Iowa families and businesses.

The post Listening, Learning, and Bringing the Taxpayer’s Voice to Local Government appeared first on ITR Foundation.

item.title: [Itrfoundation] A Primer on the Florida Property Tax Amendment
item.description:
Florida voters will decide whether to dramatically expand the homestead exemption, eliminating much of the property tax burden on many owner-occupied homes while limiting how local governments can use the remaining property tax revenue. The amendment does not apply to school district property taxes, which typically make up 40% to 50% of a Florida homeowner's property tax bill, meaning most homeowners would still pay taxes to support public schools. Taxpayers need to pay attention to how local governments respond, even as property taxes are reduced for many Floridians. Local governments may reduce spending, shift taxes to other property owners, hike other taxes and fees, or adopt some combination of those approaches.

The post A Primer on the Florida Property Tax Amendment appeared first on ITR Foundation.

item.title: [Itrfoundation] New Jersey’s Warning—and Iowa’s Continuing Duty
item.description:
New Jersey's voter registration error shows that election integrity depends on accurate systems, not just good intentions. A software glitch registered thousands of self-identified noncitizens, demonstrating how administrative failures can undermine public confidence. Iowa has strengthened safeguards, but recent audits show continued vigilance is necessary. Constitutional protections, citizenship verification, and federal database checks have improved election security, yet officials still identified a small number of ineligible registrations and ballots. The goal is both election integrity and voter access. Protecting the right of every eligible citizen to vote also requires ensuring that ineligible votes are prevented so every lawful ballot carries equal weight.

The post New Jersey’s Warning—and Iowa’s Continuing Duty appeared first on ITR Foundation.
